newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa mulls provincial housing debt write-off.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa mulls provincial housing debt write-off.

text.p: South African local authorites could have their housing debts to the central government written off as part of plans to deal with a nominal 12 billion rand in national housing assets, a senior housing department official said on Monday.

Neville Karsten, deputy director general of the department, made the remarks during a press briefing intended to clarify what had become of the assets which were the subject of a parliamentary public accounts committee meeting last month.
"The 12 billion rand has not just disappeared," he said, adding that about 10 billion rand of the money comprised loans to local authorities and the rest was a range of fixed assets.

Karsten said the 12 billion figure was purely nominal because the actual value had been eroded by, among other things, interest rates for sub-economic housing which were set well below the market level. This was a form of subsidy which did not appear on the books, he said.
"Each year the government added capital to the national housing fund to keep it alive. If it had been a business, it would have gone bankrupt," Karsten said.
Difficulties in accounting for the assets, pinpointed by the auditor general's office last month, also arose because some housing records had been destroyed in the political violence of the 1980s.

"We believe local government should administer and manage these assets," Karsten said. "We need to clear those assets and devolve them down to local government level. This has been approved in principle by the housing minister...
"This would create a potential asset base for local government... which should be ring-fenced from other local government accounts so it can be used to the advantage of the poor."
Karsten said that as part of the process, the 10 billion rand loan liability "should be extinguished from the perspective of the local government debt to the national government".
But this did not mean writing off the money owed to local authorities by individual users of the housing stock, he added.
The housing department has asked the parliamentary public accounts committee to approve the hiring of outside consultants to make a full accounting of the 12 billion rand.
